topic: How debt and an Amazon deal killed Toys R Us
title: How Toys "R" Us Was Killed by $5 Billion of Debt

Why Toys "R" Us Really Died (It Wasn't Amazon)

description:
For generations of kids, Toys "R" Us was paradise. Then, in 2018, every store in America closed. Most people blame Amazon. The real story is stranger: a deal with Amazon that backfired, and a buyout that loaded the company with billions in debt.

In this video: how Charles Lazarus invented the toy supermarket, why Toys "R" Us once paid Amazon to sell its toys, what a leveraged buyout is, and how interest payments slowly strangled the most famous toy store in the world.

• The toy supermarket and Geoffrey the giraffe
• The Amazon deal of the year 2000
• The 6.6 billion dollar buyout
• 400 million dollars a year in interest
• The closing and the comeback of the brand

segments.text: For millions of kids, there was no better place on Earth. Endless aisles of toys, bikes, video games, and a friendly giraffe called Geoffrey. Toys R Us was not just a store. It was a childhood memory. Then, in 2018, it closed every single one of its stores in the United States, and around 30,000 people lost their jobs. Most people think Amazon killed it. But the truth is much stranger. Toys R Us was killed by a deal with Amazon, and by billions of dollars of debt it did not even choose.

The story starts in 1948 in Washington, with a young man called Charles Lazarus. He opened a store selling baby furniture. It was the time of the baby boom after the Second World War, and business was good. But Lazarus noticed something. Parents bought a crib only once. But they came back again and again for toys. So he changed everything. He decided to sell toys, lots of them, in huge stores designed like supermarkets.

It was a revolutionary idea. Before that, toys were sold in small shops or in a corner of department stores, and mostly around Christmas. Lazarus built giant stores with thousands of toys, open all year, with low prices. Parents pushed shopping carts through the aisles like in a grocery store. The name, with the backwards R, looked like a child had written it. And the mascot, Geoffrey the giraffe, became one of the most famous characters in America.

For decades, Toys R Us was a machine. It expanded across America and then around the world, from Europe to Japan. At its peak, it had well over a thousand stores. It was so powerful that toy makers designed products thinking about what Toys R Us wanted. If Toys R Us did not order your toy, you were in trouble. And the famous jingle promised that kids would never have to grow up. But in the late nineties, something new appeared.

The internet. Online shopping was growing, and in the Christmas season of 1999, the Toys R Us website had serious problems delivering orders on time. Children woke up on Christmas morning without the presents their parents had ordered. Later, the Federal Trade Commission fined the company, along with other online stores, for missing delivery promises, with Toys R Us paying around 350,000 dollars. It was embarrassing, and the company decided it did not know how to do internet sales by itself. So in 2000, the company made a deal that looked smart at the time. It signed a ten year partnership with a young company that was very good at websites: Amazon. Toys R Us would be the exclusive toy seller on Amazon, and in exchange, it would pay Amazon around 50 million dollars a year plus a share of sales.

Think about that for a second. Toys R Us, the king of toys, was paying Amazon to run its online sales. Its own website simply redirected customers to Amazon. For a few years, it looked fine. But Amazon was not interested in being anybody's exclusive partner forever. It started allowing other sellers to offer toys and games on its site. Toys R Us felt betrayed and sued. In 2006 it won, and the partnership ended. But it had lost years it could never get back.

While Amazon learned everything about how people buy toys online, Toys R Us had outsourced the most important skill of the next decade. When the deal ended, it had to build its own online store almost from zero. And it was far behind. But that was not the worst decision in this story. The worst decision had already happened, and it had nothing to do with toys.

By the early 2000s, Toys R Us had big competitors: Walmart and Target, which sold toys very cheaply to bring customers into their stores. Toys R Us was still profitable, but growing slowly. And that is exactly the kind of company that attracts private equity firms. In 2005, three investment groups, KKR, Bain Capital and the real estate company Vornado, bought Toys R Us for around 6.6 billion dollars. If you like stories like this one, subscribe, because this channel is about the money behind the headlines.

But here is the key. They did not pay for most of it with their own money. This was a leveraged buyout. The buyers borrowed billions of dollars, around five billion, and then put that debt on Toys R Us itself. Imagine buying a house with a huge mortgage, and then making the house pay the mortgage. From that day, the company had to pay enormous interest every single year, around 400 million dollars annually, before it could invest a single dollar in anything else.

Four hundred million dollars a year. That is money that could have been used to renovate old stores, to hire more staff, to build a great website, or to lower prices against Walmart and Amazon. Instead, it went to lenders. Year after year, the stores started to look older. Customers complained about empty shelves and slow service. The company tried to go back to the stock market to raise money, but the plan was cancelled. Meanwhile, online shopping grew and grew.

In September 2017, just before the Christmas season, Toys R Us filed for bankruptcy. The company hoped to restructure and survive. But the holiday sales were weak, suppliers were nervous, and lenders did not believe in a comeback. In March 2018, the company announced it would close or sell all its stores in the United States. Around 30,000 employees lost their jobs, and many of them said they did not receive severance pay at first, which caused a public scandal.

The investors, on the other hand, had collected fees over the years. After public pressure, some of them created a fund of around 20 million dollars for former employees. For thousands of workers who had given years of their lives to the company, it felt like very little. The stores emptied, the Geoffrey statues disappeared, and one of the most beloved brands in America seemed dead.

The collapse also shook the whole toy industry. Toys R Us was one of the biggest customers for companies like Mattel and Hasbro. When it disappeared, those companies lost a huge sales channel overnight. Smaller toy makers suffered even more, because Toys R Us was one of the few stores willing to display a wide variety of toys, not just the bestsellers. When a giant retailer dies, it takes a lot of the ecosystem with it.

But the brand did not die completely. The name and Geoffrey were bought by new owners, and Toys R Us started coming back in a different form: small shops inside department stores like Macy's in the United States, and stores in other countries that had been sold separately. It is a very different business, much smaller. But for many adults, walking into one is still pure nostalgia.

So, did Amazon kill Toys R Us? Partly, yes. But not the way people think. Toys R Us made two fatal mistakes. First, it handed its online future to the company that would become its biggest competitor. Second, its new owners loaded it with debt at the exact moment it needed money to change. A company can survive a strong competitor. It is much harder to survive a strong competitor with 400 million dollars of interest to pay every year.
Now, tell me in the comments: do you remember going to Toys R Us as a kid? What is your best memory? And who do you think is more responsible for its death: Amazon, or the investors?

segments.text: In 2000, Toys R Us paid Amazon around 50 million dollars a year to sell its toys online. Its own website just sent customers to Amazon. So Amazon learned everything about selling toys online, while Toys R Us learned nothing. Then, in 2005, investors bought the company with borrowed money and put around 5 billion dollars of debt on it. The interest alone was around 400 million dollars a year. In 2018, every American store closed. The full story is on the channel.
